summary: Practice stack, tree-encoding, and dynamic-programming prompts aligned with Microsoft-style interviews.

questions.title: Min Stack
questions.summary: Design a stack that can return the current minimum in constant time.
questions.prompt: Implement push, pop, top, and getMin so getMin returns the smallest value currently in the stack.

examples.input: push(-2), push(0), push(-3), getMin(), pop(), getMin()
examples.explanation: The minimum changes after -3 is removed.

constraints: All primary operations should be constant time.

solutionTracks.title: Value Stack Plus Min Stack
solutionTracks.summary: Keep normal values in one stack and the minimum at each depth in a parallel stack.

steps.title: Push current minimum
steps.explanation: When a value is pushed, also push the smaller of that value and the previous minimum.

steps.title: Pop both stacks
steps.explanation: Removing a value also removes the minimum snapshot for that stack depth.

steps.title: Read min top
steps.explanation: The top of the min stack is always the minimum across all active values.

solutionTracks.explanation: The min stack mirrors the value stack. Each depth stores the minimum for exactly the values below or at that depth, so getMin is a top lookup.

solutionTracks.title: Encoded Delta Stack
solutionTracks.summary: Store differences from the current minimum so a single stack can recover previous minimum values.

steps.title: Store value minus min
steps.explanation: A negative delta means the pushed value became the new minimum.

steps.title: Update min on negative push
steps.explanation: When the delta is negative, set min to the new value after saving the delta.

steps.title: Restore on negative pop
steps.explanation: A negative popped delta tells how to reconstruct the previous minimum.

solutionTracks.explanation: The delta encodes whether the minimum changed at that depth. Negative deltas carry enough information to restore the old minimum when that new minimum is removed.

questions.title: Serialize And Deserialize Binary Tree
questions.summary: Convert a binary tree to a string and reconstruct the same tree later.
questions.prompt: Design a serializer and deserializer for a binary tree so the decoded tree has the same values and shape as the original.
constraints: The serialized format only needs to be understood by your own deserializer.

solutionTracks.title: Preorder With Null Markers
solutionTracks.summary: Write each node before its children and include null markers so the shape can be reconstructed exactly.

steps.title: Emit node then children
steps.explanation: Preorder writes value, left subtree, then right subtree.

steps.title: Include nulls
steps.explanation: Null markers distinguish missing children from future sibling values.

steps.title: Read recursively
steps.explanation: Deserialization consumes the stream in the same preorder and rebuilds each subtree.

solutionTracks.explanation: Values alone cannot identify where missing children belonged. Null markers make the serialized stream a complete description of both tree values and tree shape.

solutionTracks.title: Level Order With Markers
solutionTracks.summary: Serialize the tree breadth-first so positions line up with a common array representation.

steps.title: Queue nodes
steps.explanation: Process nodes breadth-first and write each value as it leaves the queue.

steps.title: Write null children
steps.explanation: When a child is missing, write a marker so later positions remain aligned.

steps.title: Rebuild by pairs
steps.explanation: During decode, each non-null queued parent consumes the next two tokens as left and right children.

solutionTracks.explanation: Level-order serialization mirrors heap-style tree layout. Null markers are what keep sparse trees from shifting children into the wrong parent positions.

questions.title: Longest Valid Parentheses
questions.summary: Return the length of the longest well-formed parentheses substring.
questions.prompt: Given a string containing only opening and closing parentheses, return the length of the longest contiguous substring that is valid.

solutionTracks.title: Index Stack Sentinel
solutionTracks.summary: Use a stack of indexes where the top represents the boundary before the current valid substring.

steps.title: Start with sentinel
steps.explanation: Push -1 so a valid substring starting at zero can measure its length.

steps.title: Push opens
steps.explanation: Opening parentheses become possible future matches and are stored by index.

steps.title: Pop on closes
steps.explanation: After popping a match, the current valid length is current index minus the new stack top; an empty stack gets reset to current index.

solutionTracks.explanation: The stack stores boundaries that cannot be crossed by the current valid suffix. Measuring from the current index to the nearest boundary gives the longest valid suffix ending here.

solutionTracks.title: Dynamic Programming By Ending Index
solutionTracks.summary: Let dp[i] store the longest valid substring ending at index i and extend it when a close can match an earlier open.

steps.title: Only close can end valid text
steps.explanation: If the current character is open, dp at that position remains zero.

steps.title: Find matching open
steps.explanation: For a close, jump left over the previous valid suffix to locate a possible matching open.

steps.title: Add previous block
steps.explanation: If a match exists, include the inner valid suffix and any valid block immediately before the match.

solutionTracks.explanation: The DP state focuses on valid substrings ending exactly at each index. Looking behind the previous valid suffix finds whether the current close can wrap it into a longer valid substring.
